meta.title: The $20 Billion App Accused of Being a Casino
meta.working_title: Your Favourite YouTubers Promote This App. Lawyers Call It a Casino
meta.device: A golden 'chase card' (a glowing gold trading card with a star, no real logos) appears in every act, and a SWIPE TO BID pill button keeps sliding in at moments of temptation. Running tracker in act 5: a red SPENT counter in the top-left corner.
meta.style: Stormi 2D house style (Gumball-style rig characters on painted plates, same engine as Prime/Pattinson/Gulf Kings). Plates: livestream card-break studio, card shop, car showroom, auction house, tech HQ atrium, law office, basement full of card boxes, support-group room, Chinese live-commerce studio, plus reused kitchen at night, courtroom, teen room, podcast room, stadium, Westminster, Asia map. Real people stylised, no likeness, no real logos (no Whatnot, NBA or team logos). Allegations always phrased as allegations; Whatnot's replies shown.
meta.source: YouTube reference (Fern, 'The Worst New YouTube Sponsor', youtu.be/wA2DRkzGfr4, transcript pulled via Pushpam's Chrome 27 Nov 2026), itself based on Wall Street Journal and New York Times reporting. Research only; original script, en-GB.

shots.vo: One evening in February twenty twenty-five, a man spent twenty-five thousand dollars on a single purchase. Not a car. Not a deposit on a house. A spot in a live stream, for a chance at some trading cards.
shots.visual: Night kitchen; a man (Sean) hunched over his phone at the table; a SWIPE TO BID pill slides under his thumb; a counter rockets to $25,000.
shots.anim: Phone glow on his face; counter rolls up; card fan flutters on screen.

shots.vo: No warning popped up. Nobody called. The app simply sent an email: thank you for your purchase.
shots.visual: Close on the phone: an email card slides in 'Thank you for your purchase!'; no warning icon appears (a crossed-out warning triangle).
shots.anim: Email ping; a warning triangle tries to pop up and is crossed out.

shots.vo: That app is Whatnot. It only launched in twenty nineteen, it's now valued at twenty billion dollars, and chances are your favourite YouTubers have promoted it.
shots.visual: Gleaming tech HQ atrium; a giant screen counter climbs to $20 BILLION; creator figures with phones and ring lights wave.
shots.anim: Counter climbs; confetti; creators wave phones.

shots.vo: But lawyers and former users are now asking an awkward question. Is Whatnot really a shopping app? Or, as some allege, a casino that nobody licensed?
shots.visual: Courtroom: a lawyer holds up a trading card like evidence; a slot-machine reel made of cards spins on a screen behind.
shots.anim: Gavel tap; slot reels of cards spin and stop on a question mark.

shots.vo: So what is really going on inside Whatnot?
shots.visual: Title over the golden chase card spinning slowly under a spotlight, a phone screen behind it.
shots.anim: Golden card spins and glints; title slams in.

shots.vo: Imagine eBay and TikTok had a baby. You scroll through endless live streams, and in each one somebody is selling something in real time. Trainers, coins, toys, designer bags. And, above all, trading cards.
shots.visual: A livestream card studio: shelves of sealed card boxes, ring lights, a host at a desk; floating phone frames scroll past with trainers, coins, a toy, a handbag, cards.
shots.anim: Phone frames scroll upwards; host waves at camera; ring lights flicker.

shots.vo: Anyone can sell. You open a shop, go live, and Whatnot takes a cut of up to eight per cent. It runs in America, Canada, Australia, several EU countries, and here in the UK.
shots.visual: A seller in a home studio sets up a camera on a tripod; coins flow from buyers, 8% of them peel off to a little vault; small flags (plain colour) pop up: US, CA, AU, EU, UK.
shots.anim: Seller adjusts camera; coin stream splits; UK tile pops last with a ding.

shots.vo: But the real action is something called a box break. A seller opens a sealed box of cards live on camera, and viewers buy a spot: a share of whatever comes out.
shots.visual: Host slices the shrink-wrap of a sealed box; the box is divided into glowing slots, each with a viewer's avatar.
shots.anim: Knife slice; box lid lifts; slots fill with avatars.

shots.vo: In a randomised break, you don't choose your team. You pay first, and then a randomiser hands you one. Good team, great cards. Bad team, bad luck. Sometimes your team isn't even in the box.
shots.visual: A big randomiser wheel spins on the host's screen; a viewer's avatar lands on a team colour; then on a grey 'NOT IN BOX' slot; the viewer's face drops.
shots.anim: Wheel spin tick-tick-tick; stop; thumbs up then sad trombone.

shots.vo: Mystery repacks work the same way. You buy a pack without knowing what's inside, or what it's worth. The host rips it open, the chat goes wild, and somewhere, someone wins big.
shots.visual: A teenager in a bedroom watches on a laptop; host rips a pack; chat bubbles flood the screen; a gold card flashes.
shots.anim: Pack rip; chat bubbles stream up; gold flash.

shots.vo: Whatnot says every buyer must get at least one card per break, and anyone sent an empty envelope gets a refund. But remember one word: chance. This whole story hangs on it.
shots.visual: Shipping room: a padded envelope opens empty; a refund stamp thumps on it; then the word CHANCE in big letters hangs from a string and sways.
shots.anim: Envelope flap opens empty; stamp thump; word swings.

shots.vo: Back in twenty twenty-two, the whole hobby was hunting for one card. A one-of-one LeBron James card carrying logo patches from three of his teams. Collectors called it the golden ticket.
shots.visual: A busy card shop; collectors peer at a wanted poster of the golden card ('1 OF 1') on the wall; magnifying glasses.
shots.anim: Poster flutters; card glows; collectors lean in.

shots.vo: Boxes were ripped open all over the world. Even celebrities joined in, opening boxes worth six figures live online, just to find it.
shots.visual: Red-carpet style stage with camera flashes; a celebrity silhouette rips box after box; empty wrappers pile up.
shots.anim: Flashes; wrappers fly; pile grows.

shots.vo: And Whatnot made a promise. If that card was pulled in a break on its platform, the seller would win a brand new Lamborghini.
shots.visual: Glossy car showroom; a supercar (generic, no badge) on a turntable; a big ribbon bow; a seller's jaw drops.
shots.anim: Turntable rotates; spotlights sweep; bow ribbon flutters.

shots.vo: Then it actually happened. Three complete strangers, each holding a random team in a Whatnot break, watched the seller pull it. The card carried all three of their teams.
shots.visual: Livestream studio at night; host pulls a card that glows gold; three small viewer windows (three strangers) scream with joy.
shots.anim: Card slides out; gold burst; three windows shake with joy.

shots.vo: It later sold at auction for around two point four million dollars, split three ways. Life-changing money, from spots that cost a tiny fraction of that.
shots.visual: Auction house; auctioneer bangs the gavel; counter rolls to $2.4M; the sum splits into three stacks.
shots.anim: Paddles rise; gavel; counter; split into three.

shots.vo: A win like that is the best advert a platform could dream of. But in a documentary about the hunt, the presenter said it plainly: box breaks are the hobby's form of gambling.
shots.visual: Documentary set: a presenter speaks to camera; behind, a big card-box turns into a dice cube.
shots.anim: Box morphs to dice; dice tumble; presenter gestures.

shots.vo: And some now say that's not just a figure of speech. Several arbitration claims accuse Whatnot of operating, in effect, an unregulated casino, without the safeguards real casinos need.
shots.visual: Law office: a stack of claim files thumps on a desk; a lawyer reads; a casino chip rolls off the pile.
shots.anim: Files thump; chip rolls; lawyer flips pages.

shots.vo: Arbitration is a bit like a private court case, with a hired arbitrator instead of a judge. Whatnot's terms push users into it unless they opt out within thirty days. Whatnot says it's simply faster and cheaper.
shots.visual: Private wood-panelled room; an arbitrator at a desk between two parties; a door marked PRIVATE swings shut; a 30-day calendar flips.
shots.anim: Door closes; calendar pages flip; arbitrator nods.

shots.vo: One lawyer, Paul Lesko, says he represents seventy claimants. He argues that randomised breaks tick every box of an illegal lottery under California law, where Whatnot is based.
shots.visual: Lawyer at a lectern in a library; 70 small person icons fill a panel; a California-shaped wash (no borders) on a map card.
shots.anim: Icons count up to 70; lawyer taps the lectern.

shots.vo: One: consideration. You pay to get in. Two: a prize. Hosts tell you exactly what the chase card is worth. Three: chance. Which team you get is down to the randomiser.
shots.visual: Plain dark card stage: three big checkboxes tick one by one: PAY, PRIZE, CHANCE, each with a little animation (coins, golden card, wheel).
shots.anim: Three ticks land with SFX; icons animate.

shots.vo: He compares it to paying for a turkey at the supermarket, spinning a wheel at the till, and walking out with broccoli.
shots.visual: Supermarket aisle: a shopper pays for a turkey, spins a wheel at the till, and is handed broccoli; turkey waddles away.
shots.anim: Wheel spin; broccoli plop; shopper deadpan.

shots.vo: In July twenty twenty-five, a complaint in California went further, accusing Whatnot and a rival, Fanatics Live, of running unlicensed breaks. But the state didn't prosecute, and there are no criminal charges.
shots.visual: Outside a courthouse; a complaint document flutters up the steps; a big stamp 'NO CHARGES' thumps on it.
shots.anim: Paper flutters; stamp thump.

shots.vo: Whatnot rejects all of this. It says gambling isn't allowed on the platform, that rule is strictly enforced, and its randomiser uses open-source code anyone can inspect. The cases are still going on.
shots.visual: Tech HQ: a spokesperson at a podium; a code window with an open padlock floats beside; a 'CASES ONGOING' tag.
shots.anim: Code lines scroll; padlock opens; podium mic glint.

shots.vo: So what protects the people spending the money? Whatnot did add spending limits and watch-time limits. But only in December twenty twenty-five.
shots.visual: Bedroom at night; a user opens a settings screen on a big floating phone; sliders for SPEND LIMIT and WATCH LIMIT slide in; date tag.
shots.anim: Sliders slide; date tag pops.

shots.vo: And there are gaps. Ten dollars under your limit, you can still bid a hundred, and it goes through. Bids are binding, Whatnot says, like any auction. And the limit can be raised right before you hit it.
shots.visual: Chart card: a limit bar with a red line; a $100 bid block sails straight over the line; a hand drags the line higher.
shots.anim: Block sails over line with a whoosh; line dragged up.

shots.vo: You have to be eighteen to hold an account. But with permission, a thirteen-year-old can use a parent's. And the younger someone meets gambling, the higher the risk of problems later on.
shots.visual: Living room: a parent hands a phone to a 13-year-old; a badge 18+ flips to show 13 underneath; a risk arrow climbs.
shots.anim: Badge flips; arrow climbs.

shots.vo: Then there's the design. You swipe to bid. A countdown ticks. The chat cheers you on, and the host is hyping the next pack before the last one has even landed.
shots.visual: Podcast-style stream room: host hypes; a giant SWIPE TO BID pill; a red countdown 5-4-3; chat hearts and fire emojis stream.
shots.anim: Countdown ticks; swipe; chat floods.

shots.vo: Experts call these dark patterns: design that nudges you into choices you might not make with a clear head. Digital law expert Dr Mark Leiser says the pressure adds up to a degradation of consent.
shots.visual: Lecture hall/studio: an academic at a whiteboard; a phone screen with hidden strings pulling a thumb like a puppet.
shots.anim: Puppet strings tug the thumb; marker squeak.

shots.vo: He'd like your running total always on screen, warnings before big bids, and more friction when spending suddenly speeds up. A click, he says, shows what you did. Not whether you had a fair chance to decide.
shots.visual: Same expert beside a big phone mock-up: a TOTAL SPENT banner, a WARNING pop-up, a 3-step lock; a cursor click becomes a question mark.
shots.anim: Banner slides; pop-up; lock clicks three times.

shots.vo: Whatnot says its account controls let every buyer see their total spend and set limits. But it didn't answer whether it flags rapid, repeated purchases.
shots.visual: Tech HQ: spokesperson; a 'TOTAL SPEND' panel; a red flag icon tries to rise and stays half-mast with a question mark.
shots.anim: Flag wobbles half-mast; question mark pulses.

shots.vo: Sean collected baseball cards as a boy. In his forties, he fell back in love with the hobby. And in October twenty twenty-four, someone told him about Whatnot.
shots.visual: Card shop in warm light: grown-up Sean grins at a display case; a flashback bubble shows a boy with a baseball glove and cards.
shots.anim: Flashback bubble pops; SPENT tracker appears at $0.

shots.vo: At first it was single cards, maybe a hundred or two a week. It felt like a game on his phone. Then he moved into breaks and unopened packs, and the spending started to climb.
shots.visual: Sean on a sofa with his phone; single cards drop in one by one; then the phone shows a randomiser wheel; SPENT counter starts climbing.
shots.anim: Cards drop; wheel spins; counter ticks.

shots.vo: Within about three months, he says, his credit cards and personal loans were maxed out. Then a streamer offered him a deal to fill a break, and he reached for his company card.
shots.visual: Office: Sean at his work desk; credit cards stack with MAXED stamps; a chat bubble 'deal for you?'; his hand slides a company card from a drawer.
shots.anim: Stamps thump; drawer slides; card glints.

shots.vo: His order emails tell the story. Six dollars. Fourteen. Then four hundred and fifty. Two thousand. Six thousand. And on his last day, twenty-five thousand dollars on a single purchase. No flag.
shots.visual: Kitchen at night: printed order emails fan out on the table, amounts growing; the last one is huge; a flag icon stays down.
shots.anim: Papers slide one by one; amounts pop; SPENT tracker jumps.

shots.vo: In total, Sean estimates he spent around one point four million dollars on the platform. The cards he won mostly ended up in boxes in his basement. He says the thrill was the process, not the cards.
shots.visual: Dim basement: towers of card boxes; Sean stands small among them; SPENT tracker reads ~$1.4M.
shots.anim: Boxes stack higher; bulb sways; dust motes.

shots.vo: Gambling counsellors call this chasing the dragon: trying to recreate one huge win, however long the odds. And Zachary Kapp, one of those three golden-ticket winners, has said his use spiralled until he checked into rehab.
shots.visual: Support-group room: chairs in a circle; a paper dragon with a golden card in its mouth flies just out of reach of a hand.
shots.anim: Dragon swoops; hand reaches; misses.

shots.vo: Another of the three, Kevin Parker, is suing Whatnot, alleging an illegal gambling enterprise. His lawsuit says he spent over ten million dollars and lost about ninety-eight per cent of it. Whatnot wouldn't comment on any individual case.
shots.visual: Courtroom: a lawsuit binder; a pie chart 98% red; a 'NO COMMENT' tag on a podium.
shots.anim: Pie fills red; binder thump; tag swings.

shots.vo: Live shopping didn't start in America. China's Taobao Live launched in twenty sixteen, and by twenty twenty, hundreds of millions of people were buying through live streams.
shots.visual: Asia map: a glowing pulse over eastern China grows into a swarm of tiny phone icons; counter 2016 to 2020.
shots.anim: Pulses ripple; phone icons multiply.

shots.vo: But then China tightened the rules. Sellers must be verified. Popular streams are monitored. And card unboxings must show the odds before every single draw. Since February twenty twenty-six, platforms face fines and suspensions.
shots.visual: Chinese live-commerce studio: hosts with products; an inspector with a clipboard; an ODDS board (1 in 500) lights up beside a card box.
shots.anim: Clipboard ticks; odds board flips.

shots.vo: In the UK, the US and the EU, the rules are still catching up. Hobby sellers can slip past consumer law, and randomised breaks sit in the same grey zone as video game loot boxes.
shots.visual: Westminster-style hall: an official squints at a card box and a loot-box chest side by side; a grey fog rolls between them.
shots.anim: Fog rolls; official scratches head.

shots.vo: Meanwhile, Whatnot is booming. MrBeast hosted a stream on Super Bowl Sunday. Logan Paul is an early investor. And Whatnot says twenty million new users joined in twenty twenty-five alone.
shots.visual: Stadium at night: giant screen with a stream; two stylised creator figures with name tags; a user counter rockets to 20 MILLION.
shots.anim: Fireworks; counter; crowd waves.

shots.vo: Search the hashtag Whatnot partner and you'll find thousands of creator ads. Free credit. Giveaway laptops. Swipe and win. Many of those creators may have no idea about the breaks, or the lawsuits.
shots.visual: A creator's bedroom studio: a YouTuber holds up a laptop giveaway; floating #PARTNER tags multiply; a tiny lawsuit paper drifts behind them unnoticed.
shots.anim: Tags multiply; laptop sparkle; paper drifts.

shots.vo: Whatnot says gambling isn't allowed, and none of these allegations has been proven. As for Sean, he deleted the app, joined a support group, and hasn't bought a single break in almost two hundred days.
shots.visual: Support-group room in morning light: Sean stands up, deletes the app (icon shatters), a day counter ticks to ~200.
shots.anim: App icon shatters gently; day counter climbs; group claps.

shots.vo: So next time someone offers you a free laptop to download an app, remember the golden card. For every winner in a break, plenty of others paid for the chance. And if gambling or spending is hurting you, please reach out. Help is free, and it's in the description.
shots.visual: Back in the card studio, empty and dim; the golden card lies on the table beside a pile of empty wrappers; then end card.
shots.anim: Camera pushes onto the golden card; lights fade; end card.

hooks: Your favourite YouTubers promote this app. Lawyers call it a casino
Three strangers won $2.4M from a live stream. Then it went wrong

reels: Pay, prize, chance: the lottery test

fixes: All legal claims phrased as allegations; Whatnot's replies included (gambling not allowed, randomiser open-source, account controls, arbitration faster/cheaper, refunds for empty envelopes).
Celebrity box-opening kept generic (source names a rapper); MrBeast and Logan Paul stylised, no likeness.
LeBron card shown as a generic gold 1-of-1 card, no NBA or team logos.
Sean's timeline: source says Oct 2024 start, maxed out by Dec/Jan, $25k single purchase on his last day (Feb 2025), ~$1.4M total spent (source wording 'Oct 2024-Mar 2026'); phrased 'he estimates'.
Kevin Parker suit (Nov 2025): over $10M purchases, ~98% lost, per the lawsuit; Zachary Kapp rehab per NYT May 2026 interview, phrased 'has said'.
cuts: Original script in our own words (source ~6,000 words, ours ~1,450).
Cut: Hostinger ad, Grant LaFontaine quotes, 2018 sports betting ruling and Utah angle, Reddit ban tactics, GA vs Collectors MD detail.
UK angle added: Whatnot runs in the UK; UK rules lag; help links include UK services.
